relatedPassages.exactPassage: "Look at this," she says, pointing at the difference between starting at 20 and starting at 30. "Same R500 a month. Start at 20, you have over R2 million. Start at 30, you have R1.1 million. The difference is not the money you put in. You put in R60,000 more if you start at 20. The difference is the TIME. Those ten extra years of compounding are worth over R1 million. Time is the ingredient you cannot buy. You either have it or you do not. And you —" she points at Myah "— you have it. I did not. I learned this at 65. You are learning it at 16. Do not waste it."
Every five years you delay costs you hundreds of thousands — not because you save less, but because you lose compounding time.

Key idea: Gogo Maria's table does not lie. R500 a month from age 20 becomes R2.3 million. The same R500 from age 30 becomes R1.1 million. The difference is not the money. The difference is the time. Time is the ingredient you cannot buy more of. You either start early or you pay for the delay — in rands, in freedom, in options. The math is indifferent to your feelings. It does not care if you are ready. It only cares if you start.

entries.exactPassage: "One: it must be in writing. Oral wills are not valid in South Africa, except in very specific limited circumstances — and even then, they are often challenged. Two: it must be signed by you — the testator. Three: it must be signed by two witnesses. These witnesses cannot be beneficiaries. If you leave something to your witness, that gift is void. Four: you must be of sound mind when you sign it. You must understand what you are doing and the consequences of your decisions."
entries.concern: The four points omit competence age and signing/presence details. A beneficiary should not witness because benefit disqualification can result, with exceptions; this is not automatically whole-will invalidity or an unconditional void-gift rule.
entries.proposedWording: Use the Justice guidance as an introductory reference: competent maker16+, writing, appropriate testator signing and competent witnesses14+with the required presence/signing formalities. A beneficiary should not witness because benefit disqualification may result, subject to exceptions. Do not describe these points as a complete legal checklist or the classroom draft as a valid will.

relatedPassages.exactPassage: [["Requirement", "Why It Matters"], ["In writing", "Oral wills generally not valid"], ["Signed by testator", "Proves it is your will and your wishes"], ["Signed by two witnesses", "Confirms you signed willingly and were of sound mind"], ["Witnesses cannot be beneficiaries", "Prevents conflict of interest — protects the integrity of the will"]]

Here’s the tension: a will is both powerful and fragile. Powerful because it directs your entire legacy. Fragile because a single mistake — a witness who is also a beneficiary, a missing signature, unclear language — can invalidate the whole document. The law is precise. It does not care about your intentions if your execution is flawed. The lesson is not just "make a will." The lesson is "make a will correctly." Get advice. Follow the rules. Do not let a technicality undo your final act of love.
Question 1: What are the four requirements for a valid will in South Africa? Why can a beneficiary not be a witness?

entries.exactPassage: She pauses. "If you break any of these rules, your will can be challenged. It can be declared invalid. And if your will is invalid, you die intestate — without a valid will. And when you die intestate, the government decides who gets your things. Not your family. Not your wishes. The government. There is a law called the Intestate Succession Act. It has a formula. It does not know your family. It does not know who you loved. It does not know who needs what. It just applies the formula."
entries.concern: The repeated contrast suggests government chooses personally. A valid will and intestacy are legal processes with rules and exceptions, rather than personal wishes versus arbitrary government discretion.
entries.proposedWording: If no valid will governs the estate, applicable intestate-succession law determines distribution. That result may differ from personal wishes, but follows law rather than an official’s preference. The exact result needs relevant family/legal facts.
